Tail Class Catalog

Main facts¶

The SCoFT Prologue guide separates Gaussian-relative kurtosis from asymptotic tail classes. This catalog compares nonnegative right-tail models by subexponentiality and regular variation, then checks which moments exist. The definitions concern a specified population law.

The positive classifications are cited, not proved here: Foss, Korshunov, and Zachary, second edition (2013), §3.5, Theorem 3.29 and its following paragraph, p. 57 (regular variation, including Pareto); Theorem 3.30 and its following examples, p. 58 (lognormal and Weibull with shape below one). See Foss et al. (2013). We derive the elementary tail ratios and moment contrasts below; the appendix proves the convolution decomposition.

Let Fˉ(x)=P(X>x)\bar F(x)=\mathbb P(X>x)Fˉ(x)=P(X>x) be the survival function. In the table, “regularly varying” means Fˉ∈RV−α\bar F\in RV_{-\alpha}Fˉ∈RV−α​ for some α>0\alpha>0α>0, so Fˉ(tx)/Fˉ(x)→t−α\bar F(tx)/\bar F(x)\to t^{-\alpha}Fˉ(tx)/Fˉ(x)→t−α for fixed t>0t>0t>0. Here FFF is the CDF, xxx is the threshold, and α\alphaα is a positive tail exponent. All models in this table have nonnegative support, with positive scale parameters, positive gamma shape and rate, and nonzero lognormal log-variance. See Shared notation.

DistributionSubexponential?Regularly varying?Diagnostic tail behavior
Pareto, Fˉ(x)=(xm/x)α\bar F(x)=(x_m/x)^\alphaFˉ(x)=(xm​/x)αYesYesExact power tail.
LognormalYesNoHeavier than any exponential, lighter than any power.
Weibull, Fˉ(x)=exp⁡(−xβ)\bar F(x)=\exp(-x^\beta)Fˉ(x)=exp(−xβ) with 0<β<10<\beta<10<β<1YesNoStretched exponential tail.
ExponentialNoNoMemoryless light tail.

For the lognormal row, “heavier than any exponential, lighter than any power” means the survival function satisfies

(1)

The inclusion direction to remember is:

Fˉ∈RV−α, α>0⟹F is subexponential,\bar F\in RV_{-\alpha},\ \alpha>0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad F\text{ is subexponential},Fˉ∈RV−α​, α>0⟹F is subexponential,
(2)

for distributions supported on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞). The converse fails: lognormal and stretched-Weibull tails are subexponential without being regularly varying.

Slow variation need not settle to a constant¶

SCoFT v4 §§2.2.1 and 2.2.11, pp. 9 and 13, discuss a practical transition to a nearly constant tail factor Taleb, 2025. Such a transition is an extra modeling assumption. The definition of slow variation does not imply a finite constant limit, or an exact Pareto tail beyond a finite threshold.

Here is a complete counterexample, in dimensionless units:

Fˉ(x)={1,x<1,x−2(1+log⁡x),x≥1.\bar F(x)= \begin{cases} 1,&x<1,\\ x^{-2}(1+\log x),&x\ge1. \end{cases}Fˉ(x)={1,x−2(1+logx),​x<1,x≥1.​
(3)

We prove that this is a survival function with a regularly varying tail. It is continuous at 1, tends to zero at infinity, and its derivative on x>1x>1x>1 is −x−3(1+2log⁡x)<0-x^{-3}(1+2\log x)<0−x−3(1+2logx)<0. Thus it defines a probability law on [1,∞)[1,\infty)[1,∞). Its factor L(x)=1+log⁡xL(x)=1+\log xL(x)=1+logx tends to infinity, while for every fixed t>0t>0t>0 and sufficiently large xxx,

L(tx)L(x)=1+log⁡t1+log⁡x⟶1,Fˉ(tx)Fˉ(x)⟶t−2.\frac{L(tx)}{L(x)}=1+\frac{\log t}{1+\log x}\longrightarrow1, \qquad \frac{\bar F(tx)}{\bar F(x)}\longrightarrow t^{-2}.L(x)L(tx)​=1+1+logxlogt​⟶1,Fˉ(x)Fˉ(tx)​⟶t−2.
(4)

The chapter 2 worked cases evaluate this ratio alongside the exact Pareto ratio 1/41/41/4 at multiplier 2. A finite curve cannot establish where a tail approximation becomes adequate; threshold selection requires its own diagnostics. The example disproves a constant-limit requirement analytically.

Moment gates are different questions¶

The Cramér condition asks whether EeθX<∞\mathbb E e^{\theta X}<\inftyEeθX<∞ for at least one θ>0\theta>0θ>0. Ordinary moments ask about EXq\mathbb E X^qEXq, with q>0q>0q>0. For the following nonnegative models:

ModelFinite positive power momentsFinite positive exponential moments
Exponential, rate 1Every q>0q>0q>0Exactly 0<θ<10<\theta<10<θ<1
Lognormal, log⁡X∼N(0,1)\log X\sim N(0,1)logX∼N(0,1)Every q>0q>0q>0None
Pareto Type I, α>0\alpha>0α>0, xm>0x_m>0xm​>0Exactly 0<q<α0<q<\alpha0<q<αNone

The Pareto moment proof gives the last row’s power-moment boundary, including divergence at q=αq=\alphaq=α; the Cramér note proves its exponential-moment failure. For the exponential row, direct integration gives ∫0∞xqe−x dx=Γ(q+1)<∞\int_0^\infty x^q e^{-x}\,dx=\Gamma(q+1)<\infty∫0∞​xqe−xdx=Γ(q+1)<∞ and ∫0∞e−(1−θ)x dx=1/(1−θ)\int_0^\infty e^{-(1-\theta)x}\,dx=1/(1-\theta)∫0∞​e−(1−θ)xdx=1/(1−θ) when θ<1\theta<1θ<1; the latter integral diverges when θ≥1\theta\ge1θ≥1. Here Γ\GammaΓ denotes the gamma integral.

Proof of the lognormal moment contrast¶

We prove both entries in the lognormal row. Let log⁡X∼N(0,1)\log X\sim N(0,1)logX∼N(0,1). In the log-size coordinate z=log⁡xz=\log xz=logx, completing the square gives, for every real qqq,

EXq=12π∫−∞∞eqz−z2/2 dz=eq2/212π∫−∞∞e−(z−q)2/2 dz=eq2/2.\mathbb E X^q =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{qz-z^2/2}\,dz =e^{q^2/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-(z-q)^2/2}\,dz =e^{q^2/2}.EXq=2π​1​∫−∞∞​eqz−z2/2dz=eq2/22π​1​∫−∞∞​e−(z−q)2/2dz=eq2/2.
(5)

In contrast, for any fixed θ>0\theta>0θ>0,

EeθX=12π∫−∞∞exp⁡(θez−z2/2) dz=∞.\mathbb E e^{\theta X} =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp(\theta e^z-z^2/2)\,dz=\infty.EeθX=2π​1​∫−∞∞​exp(θez−z2/2)dz=∞.
(6)

Indeed, ez/z2→∞e^z/z^2\to\inftyez/z2→∞ as z→∞z\to\inftyz→∞, so the integrand is at least 1 for all sufficiently large zzz. The integral over that half-line diverges. This establishes failure of the Cramér condition despite all positive power moments being finite. Subexponentiality is a separate, cited result; it does not follow just from this failure.

For a Pareto model with α=5/2\alpha=5/2α=5/2 and xm=1x_m=1xm​=1, the mean is 5/35/35/3 and the variance is 20/920/920/9, but the fourth moment diverges. The formulas follow from the linked integral: EX2=5\mathbb E X^2=5EX2=5 and 5−(5/3)2=20/95-(5/3)^2=20/95−(5/3)2=20/9. Pearson kurtosis is therefore not a finite summary for this model. Having a finite variance does not imply a finite fourth or positive exponential moment.

The classifications of lognormal and stretched Weibull are cited results; a ratio table is not a proof of their subexponentiality.

Exact light-tail checks¶

We prove the two negative classifications in the table. Write Gamma⁡(k,λ)\operatorname{Gamma}(k,\lambda)Gamma(k,λ) in shape–rate notation, with k,λ>0k,\lambda>0k,λ>0. At rate one, convolution of the densities with shapes kkk and ℓ>0\ell>0ℓ>0 gives

e−xΓ(k)Γ(ℓ)∫0xyk−1(x−y)ℓ−1 dy=e−xxk+ℓ−1Γ(k+ℓ),x>0,\frac{e^{-x}}{\Gamma(k)\Gamma(\ell)} \int_0^x y^{k-1}(x-y)^{\ell-1}\,dy =\frac{e^{-x}x^{k+\ell-1}}{\Gamma(k+\ell)},\qquad x>0,Γ(k)Γ(ℓ)e−x​∫0x​yk−1(x−y)ℓ−1dy=Γ(k+ℓ)e−xxk+ℓ−1​,x>0,
(9)

using the beta integral (NIST DLMF, Eq. 5.12.1). Thus independent shapes add. Scaling by 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ gives the same rule at a common rate λ\lambdaλ. The survival integral, compared with its leading integrand by l’Hôpital’s rule, gives

Fˉ(x)∼(λx)k−1e−λxΓ(k),x→∞.\bar F(x)\sim\frac{(\lambda x)^{k-1}e^{-\lambda x}}{\Gamma(k)}, \qquad x\to\infty.Fˉ(x)∼Γ(k)(λx)k−1e−λx​,x→∞.
(10)

For completeness, at rate one the derivatives of ∫x∞yk−1e−y dy\int_x^\infty y^{k-1}e^{-y}\,dy∫x∞​yk−1e−ydy and xk−1e−xx^{k-1}e^{-x}xk−1e−x have ratio [1−(k−1)/x]−1→1[1-(k-1)/x]^{-1}\to1[1−(k−1)/x]−1→1; both functions tend to zero. Consequently, for fixed t>1t>1t>1,

At(x)∼tk−1e−λ(t−1)x→0,R(x)∼Γ(k)2Γ(2k)(λx)k→∞.A_t(x)\sim t^{k-1}e^{-\lambda(t-1)x}\to0,\qquad R(x)\sim\frac{\Gamma(k)}{2\Gamma(2k)}(\lambda x)^k\to\infty.At​(x)∼tk−1e−λ(t−1)x→0,R(x)∼2Γ(2k)Γ(k)​(λx)k→∞.
(11)

A finite model comparison¶

Use pareto_type1, log_survival_multiplier_ratio.

from scipy.stats import expon, lognorm
from xmath.incerto.distributions import pareto_type1
from xmath.incerto.tail_classes import log_survival_multiplier_ratio

for label, law in (("Pareto", pareto_type1(2.5)),
                   ("Lognormal", lognorm(1)), ("Exponential", expon())):
    log_ratio = log_survival_multiplier_ratio(law.logsf, [2, 10, 100])
    print(f"{label}: [" + ", ".join(f"{v:.4g}" for v in log_ratio) + "]")

Output

Pareto: [-1.733, -1.733, -1.733]
Lognormal: [-1.081, -2.052, -3.563]
Exponential: [-2, -10, -100]

A finite grid illustrates the specified laws and cannot classify unknown data.

Figure regeneration: uv run python demos/incerto/prologue_tail_classes.py from the repository root. It evaluates log⁡A2(u)\log A_2(u)logA2​(u) for Pareto (α=5/2,xm=1)(\alpha=5/2,x_m=1)(α=5/2,xm​=1), standard lognormal, Weibull (β=1/2)(\beta=1/2)(β=1/2), exponential (rate 1), and gamma (shape 2, rate 1). The fixed grid has 241 logarithmically spaced thresholds from 1 to 104; all quantities are dimensionless population calculations. There is no sampling, data fitting, truncation of a distribution, or uncertainty interval.

The script also prints exact exponential and gamma two-sum checks at u=2,10,100u=2,10,100u=2,10,100. The helper uses log survival values for the multiplier figure; non-finite values cause an error. In particular, it does not divide zeros when an ordinary survival function underflows. The figure is numerical illustration of the formulas above, not evidence of an observed tail class.

A survival that varies slowly itself¶

The positive-exponent convention in the table does not exhaust regularly varying functions. To examine the index-zero boundary, let VVV be Pareto with minimum vm>0v_m>0vm​>0, exponent a>0a>0a>0, and dimensionless values, and put X=eVX=e^VX=eV. Here a,vma,v_ma,vm​ are local parameters; the survival exponent of XXX will be zero. This construction is motivated by SCoFT v4 §5.5, pp. 102–103 Taleb, 2025. Inverting the increasing transform gives its survival Fˉ\bar FFˉ; differentiating gives its Lebesgue density fff:

Fˉ(x)=P(X>x)=(vmlog⁡x)a,x≥evm,f(x)=avmax(log⁡x)a+1.\bar F(x)=P(X>x)=\left(\frac{v_m}{\log x}\right)^a,\quad x\ge e^{v_m}, \qquad f(x)=\frac{a v_m^a}{x(\log x)^{a+1}}.Fˉ(x)=P(X>x)=(logxvm​​)a,x≥evm​,f(x)=x(logx)a+1avma​​.
(13)

For every fixed t>0t>0t>0, its survival ratio tends to one because log⁡(tx)/log⁡x→1\log(tx)/\log x\to1log(tx)/logx→1. Thus Fˉ∈RV0\bar F\in RV_0Fˉ∈RV0​, outside this catalog’s positive-power rows. Every positive power moment diverges: EXp=EepV\mathbb EX^p=\mathbb E e^{pV}EXp=EepV, and the exponential factor eventually exceeds every polynomial in the Pareto density integral.

We also prove subexponentiality directly for this example. For iid copies X1,X2X_1,X_2X1​,X2​ of this nonnegative XXX, with M2=max⁡(X1,X2)M_2=\max(X_1,X_2)M2​=max(X1​,X2​),

P(M2>x)≤P(X1+X2>x)≤P(M2>x/2).P(M_2>x)\le P(X_1+X_2>x)\le P(M_2>x/2).P(M2​>x)≤P(X1​+X2​>x)≤P(M2​>x/2).
(14)

Both bounds divided by 2Fˉ(x)2\bar F(x)2Fˉ(x) tend to one: the maximum-tail formula is 2Fˉ(x)−Fˉ(x)22\bar F(x)-\bar F(x)^22Fˉ(x)−Fˉ(x)2 and Fˉ(x/2)/Fˉ(x)→1\bar F(x/2)/\bar F(x)\to1Fˉ(x/2)/Fˉ(x)→1. The squeeze proves the claim. Thus a regularly varying survival can be subexponential even when its index is zero. There is no finite positive 1/α1/\alpha1/α calibration at this index-zero boundary.

The chapter demo evaluates this survival using log⁡x=2,4,8\log x=2,4,8logx=2,4,8 with a=2a=2a=2, vm=1v_m=1vm​=1, obtaining 1/4,1/16,1/641/4,1/16,1/641/4,1/16,1/64. It keeps the thresholds in logarithmic coordinates to avoid overflowing eVe^VeV. Finite evaluations do not stand in for the moment-divergence or convolution proofs.

The maximum-entropy note gives another construction of power tails, conditional on specified information constraints. Neither construction establishes a tail law for observed data.

Regime separation is not a tail class¶

Appendix A of SCoFT v4, §A.1, pp. 122–124 Taleb, 2025, considers distributions with separated regimes. We can check the effect on kurtosis without assuming a power tail. Let BBB take -1 and 1 with equal probabilities, let Z∼N(0,1)Z\sim N(0,1)Z∼N(0,1) be independent, and set X=mB+σZX=mB+\sigma ZX=mB+σZ, with m≥0m\ge0m≥0 and σ>0\sigma>0σ>0. Symmetry gives mean zero. Expanding and discarding the odd terms proves

EX2=m2+σ2,EX4=m4+6m2σ2+3σ4,K=3−2m4(m2+σ2)2.\mathbb EX^2=m^2+\sigma^2,\qquad \mathbb EX^4=m^4+6m^2\sigma^2+3\sigma^4, \qquad K=3-\frac{2m^4}{(m^2+\sigma^2)^2}.EX2=m2+σ2,EX4=m4+6m2σ2+3σ4,K=3−(m2+σ2)22m4​.
(15)

Here KKK is Pearson kurtosis. For m>0m>0m>0 it lies below three and tends to one as m/σ→∞m/\sigma\to\inftym/σ→∞. Yet EetX=cosh⁡(mt)eσ2t2/2<∞\mathbb E e^{tX}=\cosh(mt)e^{\sigma^2t^2/2}<\inftyEetX=cosh(mt)eσ2t2/2<∞ for every real ttt. This location mixture is light-tailed. Its density fff has a local minimum at zero when m>σm>\sigmam>σ: differentiating the two normal densities gives f′′(0)=f(0)(m2−σ2)/σ4>0f''(0)=f(0)(m^2-\sigma^2)/\sigma^4>0f′′(0)=f(0)(m2−σ2)/σ4>0. Thus low kurtosis can accompany a valley around the expectation. It is not evidence of a small probability of a large regime change.

For m=2m=2m=2, σ=1\sigma=1σ=1, the variance is 5 and K=43/25=1.72K=43/25=1.72K=43/25=1.72. The variance-mixture note holds the location fixed and mixes variances; these are different experiments. A finite normal mixture has positive density everywhere, so a valley is not a forbidden interval and every individual point still has probability zero.

An absorbing state needs repeated chances to be reached¶

For the §A.2 context, pp. 124–125, take a homogeneous two-state Markov chain with states intact and failed. The failed state is absorbing and an intact system fails with probability p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1]p∈[0,1] at each step, conditional on still being intact. Its row-stochastic transition matrix is

T=(1−pp01),Tn=((1−p)n1−(1−p)n01)(n≥1).T=\begin{pmatrix}1-p&p\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^n=\begin{pmatrix}(1-p)^n&1-(1-p)^n\\0&1\end{pmatrix} \quad(n\ge1).T=(1−p0​p1​),Tn=((1−p)n0​1−(1−p)n1​)(n≥1).
(16)

Induction proves the power: multiplying by TTT multiplies the remaining intact probability by 1−p1-p1−p. Starting intact, eventual failure has probability one if p>0p>0p>0 and zero if p=0p=0p=0. Irreversibility alone is not sufficient; reachability and persistent conditional risk matter. With varying conditional hazards pjp_jpj​, intact survival is ∏j=1n(1−pj)\prod_{j=1}^n(1-p_j)∏j=1n​(1−pj​). For example, pj=2−j−1p_j=2^{-j-1}pj​=2−j−1 has sum 1/21/21/2, and ∏j=1n(1−pj)≥1−∑j=1npj≥1/2\prod_{j=1}^n(1-p_j)\ge1-\sum_{j=1}^n p_j\ge1/2∏j=1n​(1−pj​)≥1−∑j=1n​pj​≥1/2 by induction. Every step has positive risk but eventual failure is not certain. The existing survival calculation treats this product; we do not replace it with an independence assumption on unconditional events.

Use normal_location_mixture_kurtosis, survival_from_hazards.

from xmath.incerto.multivariate import normal_location_mixture_kurtosis
from xmath.incerto.lecture_risk import survival_from_hazards

print(f"Location-mixture kurtosis: {normal_location_mixture_kurtosis(2):.4g}")
print(f"Constant hazard: {survival_from_hazards([0.05] * 100)[-1]:.4g}")
hazards = [2.0**(-j - 1) for j in range(1, 101)]
print(f"Decreasing hazard: {survival_from_hazards(hazards)[-1]:.4g}")

Output

Location-mixture kurtosis: 1.72
Constant hazard: 0.005921
Decreasing hazard: 0.5776

Neither example asserts a power-tail law.

The Pareto mixture contrast shows what changes when one regime actually has a power tail.

Caveats¶

  • Regular variation and subexponentiality concern limits, not the shape of a fitted curve on a finite range.

  • Very small survival probabilities can underflow in numerical calculations. Logarithmic ratios help preserve information; rounded zeros do not establish exact zero probability.

  • The subexponential definition used here is the right-tail iid version for nonnegative summands. Two-sided and dependent settings need additional assumptions.

  • The finite exact examples above check formulas, not the accuracy of an upstream sampler, survival-function implementation, or quadrature routine.

Appendix: convolution calculation¶

This appendix proves the elementary two-summand convolution decomposition used by the subexponential diagnostic. We work with independent variables having Lebesgue densities, then specialize to an iid lower-bounded distribution. The convolution identity also applies to two-sided laws; the subexponential definition above uses nonnegative summands. Discrete and dependent variants require separate treatment.

For independent random variables X1X_1X1​ and X2X_2X2​ with Lebesgue densities, write f1f_1f1​ for the density of X1X_1X1​ and Fˉ2\bar F_2Fˉ2​ for the survival function of X2X_2X2​. Then

P(X1+X2>x)=∫−∞∞f1(y)Fˉ2(x−y) dy.\mathbb P(X_1+X_2>x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_1(y)\bar F_2(x-y)\,dy.P(X1​+X2​>x)=∫−∞∞​f1​(y)Fˉ2​(x−y)dy.
(17)

To see the iid reduction, take a common density fff, survival function Fˉ\bar FFˉ, and lower support endpoint aaa, with x>2ax>2ax>2a. Split the event {X1+X2>x}\{X_1+X_2>x\}{X1​+X2​>x} into three cases, ignoring probability-zero boundary points: first X2≤x/2X_2\le x/2X2​≤x/2, second X1≤x/2X_1\le x/2X1​≤x/2, and third both variables exceed x/2x/2x/2. In the first case, conditioning on X2=yX_2=yX2​=y with a≤y≤x/2a\le y\le x/2a≤y≤x/2 leaves the requirement X1>x−yX_1>x-yX1​>x−y, so this part contributes ∫ax/2f(y)Fˉ(x−y) dy\int_a^{x/2} f(y)\bar F(x-y)\,dy∫ax/2​f(y)Fˉ(x−y)dy. The second case contributes the same quantity by iid symmetry. The remaining upper-right square has probability Fˉ(x/2)2\bar F(x/2)^2Fˉ(x/2)2 by independence.

For a=0a=0a=0, the partition can be recorded as disjoint regions rather than a contour plot. Boundaries have zero probability under the continuous-law assumption.

Region within {X1+X2>x}\{X_1+X_2>x\}{X1​+X2​>x}Probability contribution
0≤X2≤x/20\le X_2\le x/20≤X2​≤x/2, X1>x−X2X_1>x-X_2X1​>x−X2​∫0x/2f(y)Fˉ(x−y) dy\int_0^{x/2}f(y)\bar F(x-y)\,dy∫0x/2​f(y)Fˉ(x−y)dy
0≤X1≤x/20\le X_1\le x/20≤X1​≤x/2, X2>x−X1X_2>x-X_1X2​>x−X1​The same integral by iid symmetry
X1>x/2X_1>x/2X1​>x/2, X2>x/2X_2>x/2X2​>x/2Fˉ(x/2)2\bar F(x/2)^2Fˉ(x/2)2

For iid variables with lower support endpoint aaa, symmetry gives the more useful half-line formula

P(X1+X2>x)=2∫ax/2f(y)Fˉ(x−y) dy+Fˉ(x/2)2.\mathbb P(X_1+X_2>x) = 2\int_a^{x/2} f(y)\bar F(x-y)\,dy+\bar F(x/2)^2.P(X1​+X2​>x)=2∫ax/2​f(y)Fˉ(x−y)dy+Fˉ(x/2)2.
(18)

When Fˉ(x)>0\bar F(x)>0Fˉ(x)>0, dividing by 2Fˉ(x)2\bar F(x)2Fˉ(x) yields a normalized integral:

R(x)=∫ax/2f(y)Fˉ(x−y)Fˉ(x) dy+Fˉ(x/2)22Fˉ(x)=∫ax/2exp⁡{log⁡f(y)+log⁡Fˉ(x−y)−log⁡Fˉ(x)} dy+12exp⁡{2log⁡Fˉ(x/2)−log⁡Fˉ(x)}.\begin{aligned} R(x) &=\int_a^{x/2}\frac{f(y)\bar F(x-y)}{\bar F(x)}\,dy +\frac{\bar F(x/2)^2}{2\bar F(x)}\\ &=\int_a^{x/2} \exp\{\log f(y)+\log\bar F(x-y)-\log\bar F(x)\}\,dy\\ &\quad+\frac12\exp\{2\log\bar F(x/2)-\log\bar F(x)\}. \end{aligned}R(x)​=∫ax/2​Fˉ(x)f(y)Fˉ(x−y)​dy+2Fˉ(x)Fˉ(x/2)2​=∫ax/2​exp{logf(y)+logFˉ(x−y)−logFˉ(x)}dy+21​exp{2logFˉ(x/2)−logFˉ(x)}.​
(19)

The logarithmic form applies where the factors are positive, with zero terms understood by limits. It avoids forming tiny unnormalized probabilities before taking their ratio. The decomposition is an ordinary conditioning argument; no numerical integration or executable package helper is needed for it.
